channel.description: Recent content in Kubernetes on DAWN's Blog

item.title: K8S ReplicationController Declarative Update Limitations: Why Pods Do Not Auto-Update on Template Changes
item.description: Hands-on verification of RC resources not supporting declarative updates: modifying the RC Pod image template, observing that running Pods do not update after kubectl apply, verifying that old Pods must be manually deleted to trigger new template recreation, and noting the risks of deleting all Pods directly in production.

item.title: K8S Pod Port Exposure and SVC Multi-Port Mapping in Practice: hostPort, Multi-Port Mapping and targetPort Name Matching
item.description: This article covers two things in K8S: exposing Pod ports and mapping multiple ports on a SVC. The first half uses hostPort to map container port 80 straight to 8888 on the node hosting the Pod, so external traffic reaches the container without going through a SVC; the access test from Windows succeeds, and hostPort is compared against NodePort (hostPort only works on the Pod’s node and its address follows the Pod when it moves, while NodePort is a Service that opens the same port on every node so movement does not affect access). The second half writes a Pod exposing both 80/TCP and 53/UDP, maps both through a SVC, inspects the PORT(S) column and the describe TargetPort/Endpoints, and finally patches targetPort to match by port name, verifying that the SVC keeps tracking the endpoint as long as the name is unchanged even if the container port number changes.

item.title: K8S Namespace Management in Practice: Imperative and Declarative Management, Cross-Namespace Service Access
item.description: This article walks through K8S namespace management. It starts with what namespaces do and how to tell namespaced from cluster-scoped resources (the NAMESPACED column of kubectl api-resources). Then it creates, lists, labels and deletes namespaces with imperative commands, and creates a Pod named xiuxian-v1 in both default and dawn to demonstrate isolation and the cascade delete that happens when a namespace is removed. Next it switches to declarative management: export a YAML from an existing resource and subtract from it, then apply to create a labeled namespace. Finally it puts MySQL in dawn and WordPress in kube-public, connects them using the cross-namespace short form db-svc.dawn, and lists the three ways to write a cross-namespace A record with the measured results.

item.title: K8S Pod DNS Policy and hostNetwork in Practice: A dnsPolicy Comparison
item.description: This article uses a control experiment to explain how a K8S Pod’s dnsPolicy interacts with hostNetwork. The test Pod sets hostNetwork: true and explicitly sets dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet; inside the container /etc/resolv.conf points at the cluster CoreDNS and carries the svc search domains, so db-svc, kubernetes and kube-dns all resolve. The control Pod only enables hostNetwork and leaves dnsPolicy at its ClusterFirst default; resolv.conf becomes the node’s own DNS with no search domains, and db-svc fails to resolve outright. Conclusion: once a Pod uses the host network, you must set dnsPolicy to ClusterFirstWithHostNet.

item.title: K8S in Practice: WordPress Deployment, NFS Persistence and CoreDNS Name Resolution
item.description: This article deploys WordPress on a K8S cluster and evolves it through three versions. v1 gets the basic chain working with ReplicationControllers and Services: MySQL RC to SVC ClusterIP with a pinned VIP, to WordPress RC, to SVC NodePort, finishing the installer in a browser; scaling WordPress to 3 replicas then exposes the data inconsistency caused by the lack of persistence. v2 introduces NFS shared storage so both MySQL data and the WordPress uploads directory land on NFS — after deleting the RC and letting it rebuild 3 fresh Pods, the marker files are still there, proving all replicas share the same data. v3 deploys the CoreDNS add-on so WordPress reaches the database by SVC name, and validates cluster DNS resolution three ways: from the manifests, by pinging SVC names inside a Pod, and with dig A-record lookups.

item.title: K8S Replica Control and Service Discovery in Practice: RC, ClusterIP and NodePort
item.description: This article works through replica control and service discovery in K8S. A ReplicationController declares 3 replicas; we verify its self-healing (deleting a Pod is automatically replenished) and that deleting the RC cascades to clean up the Pods it manages. Then a ClusterIP Service gives the 3 Pods spread across two nodes a single fixed entry point; with each Pod’s nginx returning its own Pod name, five consecutive requests reveal round-robin load balancing. Finally a NodePort Service exposes the workload on port 30080 of every node, reachable from outside the cluster and load balanced the same way.

item.title: K8S Troubleshooting Trio in Practice: kubectl explain, cp and logs
item.description: This article covers the three commands I reach for most when troubleshooting K8S. First build a troubleshooting test image that exits immediately, then use kubectl explain to read the OpenAPI Schema straight from the API Server and find out where a field belongs (no internet needed). Next, override the image’s default CMD with command + args in the Pod definition so a one-shot container stays running and can be inspected with exec. Finally, kubectl cp copies files both ways between the host and a Pod (config in, logs out), and kubectl logs is the first thing to check when a Pod misbehaves — it is how you track down CrashLoopBackOff.

item.title: K8S Volumes in Practice: emptyDir, hostPath and NFS
item.description: This article puts three K8S volume types to work. emptyDir is tied to the Pod lifecycle — a multi-container Pod shows both containers seeing the same data when the volume is mounted into each. hostPath mounts a host directory directly into the Pod; using Elasticsearch 7.17.16, indices survive deleting and recreating the Pod, proving single-node persistence. NFS solves cross-node sharing: configure nfs-kernel-server on the master, install nfs-common on all three nodes, deploy MySQL 8.3.0, write test data, then drift the Pod from worker01 to worker02 with the data fully intact. It closes with the selection rule: emptyDir for sharing inside a Pod, hostPath for single-node persistence, NFS (or distributed storage) when the workload must move across nodes.

item.title: K8S Core Resource Management and Pod Basics in Practice: Manifests, Multi-Container Pods, Labels and hostNetwork
item.description: This article walks through K8S core resource management and Pod basics. It starts with a cheat sheet of common resource short names and a kubectl api-resources overview, then covers routine health checks (worker node list, master components, the flannel interface and the cni0/flannel.1 virtual interfaces on each node). Next it writes single-container and multi-container Pod manifests, compares kubectl create with apply, and uses kubectl exec to enter a specific container. It then explains the difference between the declarative and imperative APIs, label create/read/update/delete plus filtering and deleting resources by label, and kubectl describe for resource details. Finally it demonstrates hostNetwork mode so a Pod shares the host network, and cleans up the lab environment.

item.title: K8S kubeadm Cluster Deployment in Practice: Harbor with a Self-Built CA and Flannel CNI
item.description: This hands-on guide builds a K8S kubeadm cluster (v1.23.17, 1 master + 2 workers, 3 nodes in total) from scratch. First install Docker on the harbor node and deploy a Harbor image registry (self-built CA issues the HTTPS certificate, harbor.yml enables port 443). Then install Docker on the three K8S nodes, configure /etc/hosts and the Docker client certificate, and verify docker login against Harbor successfully. Next prepare the nodes (disable swap, check product_uuid, configure iptables bridge traffic and the Aliyun apt repo, and install kubeadm/kubelet/kubectl), run kubeadm init on the master, configure kubeconfig, join the worker nodes, and finally deploy the Flannel CNI plugin so all three nodes become Ready, and verify cross-node Pod connectivity with curl.

item.title: Manually Deploying a Kubernetes v1.30 Cluster (via kubeadm)
item.description: A step-by-step guide to manually deploying a Kubernetes v1.30 cluster with kubeadm — covering firewall/SELinux, swap, kernel modules, Containerd, kubeadm init, worker join, Calico, and an IPVS add-on.
